Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES
Mara and Eli Chen are setting up one shared archive for photographs from their household, including pictures taken by their two children, Theo and June. The collection is currently spread across Mara's laptop, Eli's desktop, two phones, an older tablet, and several removable drives. Their goal is to bring the material together without losing the folders and context that still make sense to the family. They are not asking for a review of the pictures or a recommendation about which images to keep. Mara described the desired result as “one dependable place where we can find the original, even if we later make a smaller album for sharing.”

The laptop holds about 18,000 image files, mostly from 2012 onward, arranged in folders by year and by trips or family events. The desktop has around 7,000 more, but some of those are copies of files already on the laptop. One folder named “Camera imports - unsorted” contains roughly 1,400 files from an old camera; its timestamps are inconsistent, and the family has not checked every image. The tablet has a small set of scans of printed photographs from Mara's parents. Those scans were made in 2018, although the pictures themselves span several decades. Eli said, “Please keep the scan date from pretending to be the date the picture was taken.” The family would like the original files retained alongside any later edited versions.

The removable drives are not all in the same condition. A blue 2 TB drive contains an export from the laptop that was made last autumn; Mara believes it is complete but has not compared it with the current laptop. A silver 1 TB drive belongs to Eli and contains a folder of phone exports through March of this year. The small red drive is unreliable: it disconnected twice during a recent copy, and the family does not know whether its contents exist elsewhere. It has a folder called “June first steps” that Eli remembers as having a few videos not found on the desktop. The family wants the setup plan to account for checking these sources before treating any one copy as expendable. No one has yet chosen a second storage device or decided where it will be kept.

For new imports, Mara prefers a year-first folder structure, with event names beneath the year when an event is recognizable. Eli is concerned that moving files into newly named folders might break links in an existing slideshow project. That project uses a folder called “Summer 2019 selects” and is stored on the desktop; it includes edited copies as well as links to some originals. The children have each made a few folders of favorites, and those folder names should remain findable even if the files also appear in a more consistent archive structure. Neither parent has decided whether to reorganize older folders all at once or leave them in place and apply the new structure only to future imports.

The family has discussed access but has not settled it. Mara wants to view the collection on her laptop and phone when she is away from home. Eli would rather keep the full-resolution archive on the home network and share only selected albums. The children use tablets on the home Wi-Fi, but their parents have not decided whether they should be able to browse the complete collection or only family-approved albums. Mara said, “If we let the kids add pictures, I still want to know whose phone they came from.” They have not chosen a particular archive application, hosting service, or account arrangement. Any plan should distinguish decisions that depend on those choices from details they can settle while organizing files.

1. Some files have useful capture dates in their metadata, but others have dates altered by copying or scanning. The family does not want uncertain dates silently treated as confirmed. If an image has no reliable capture date, leave its date unresolved or identify it for review rather than guessing from a folder name. A few folders do have event names and approximate years supplied by Mara, which may help with later review but do not establish an exact day.
2. Duplicate-looking files are common, especially between the laptop and desktop, but not every similar pair is a duplicate. Some are edited versions, smaller exports, or different frames taken seconds apart. The parents want a way to identify likely duplicates before anything is removed. They have not agreed on an automatic deletion rule, and no one has compared the red drive with the other copies.
3. The current local configuration note is:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 56
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"
The note came from a small test on Eli's desktop. Mara recalls that the retention setting was chosen for that test, not as a settled family policy. The value and the remote-access setting therefore need to be presented accurately, without treating the test as approval of a final arrangement.

The family can spend a few evenings checking the old drives and sorting high-priority folders, but they do not expect to label every image before the archive is usable. They want the plan to show an order that limits the chance of losing an only copy, while making clear which pieces of work can happen later. Mara expects to scan another box of prints from her parents sometime next winter; it is not part of the current transfer. The family also takes short phone videos, including some too large to send in group chats, and wants them considered as part of the archive rather than silently left out.
